web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
book_title: Chapter 7: Why the Stock Trades Here — Market Expectations vs. Peers
title: Paying for the Ramp
question: What growth, margin and return does today's price already assume, and how does that compare with peers and with the company's own history?

epigraph.quote: In the short run, the market is a voting machine but in the long run it is a weighing machine.
epigraph.author: Ben Graham, as quoted by Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter for 1987 [106]

web_blocks.html: Data basis. The verified session cutoff is Thursday 12 November 2026: Xpro closed at ₹1,142.20 and the Nifty 50 at 25,299.35, and every price and multiple below uses that dated ledger [40][4]. A TradingView scanner after the NSE close on 13 November shows ₹1,190.10 (+4.19%) on about 0.6 times average volume [10]; it feeds only the peer table. Shares outstanding are 2.347 Cr [2]; earnings are trailing twelve months (TTM) to September 2026 [5]. Derived figures are our calculation; the 12% cost of capital is the Chapter 6 assumption.

web_blocks.caption: Valuation multiples at ₹1,142.20 (12 Nov 2026 close; our calculation)
web_blocks.takeaway: At 76x earnings the shares pay about 1.3% of their price in annual profit (EPS ÷ price, our calculation) [5][36].

web_blocks.html: These multiples sit on thin earnings: TTM sales of ₹591.8 Cr carry operating profit of ₹57.5 Cr (9.7%) and PAT of ₹34.9 Cr (5.9%). The window excludes the June 2025 quarter's ₹16.8 Cr FX loss (Chapter 6). Returns are the harder problem: Screener ROCE is 3.78% and ROE 2.80% (company RoCE 5.3-5.7% and RoE 4.6% for FY2026) against a 12% cost of capital [5][104]. On the 13 November print of ₹1,190.10 the P/E is 79.2x.

web_blocks.title: How the market has priced Xpro before

web_blocks.caption: Stock cycle by fiscal year: FY-end close, EPS and P/E (prices bonus-adjusted; Screener EPS; our calculation)
web_blocks.takeaway: From FY2023 to FY2026 the P/E rose every year while EPS fell 67% [40][5].

web_blocks.html: From April 2004 to March 2020 the shares closed between ₹8.5 (23 March 2020) and ₹55 (21 October 2010) [40]. In fiscal 2022 the close rose 20.1 times (₹48.7 to ₹977.9) while EPS rose 5.4 times, so the P/E went from 10.3x to 38.5x as dielectric earnings turned (Chapter 1); FY2019's P/E was 17.3x. The peak close was ₹1,634.4 on 17 December 2024 and the trough ₹813.0 on 13 March 2026 (-50.3% over 309 trading days); the shares rebounded to ₹1,503.6 on 2 July 2026, fell to ₹963.6 on 2 November and gained 14.6% by 12 November. Since 31 March 2023 the price is up 65% while EPS is down 67% to FY2026 and 40% on TTM (₹24.91 to ₹15.02). The whole gain is multiple expansion, about 2.7 times: the market is paying for the ramp, not for earnings delivered.

web_blocks.title: What the price already assumes: the reverse DCF

web_blocks.the_number: ₹67 Cr to ₹134 Cr of annual net profit is needed to support today's ₹2,681 Cr market value at 40x down to 20x earnings; at 25x it is about ₹107 Cr, three times the TTM ₹35 Cr.
web_blocks.how_calculated: Divide the market capitalisation (₹1,142.20 × 2.347 Cr shares) by a chosen steady-state P/E; an earnings hurdle, not a discounted cash-flow value.
web_blocks.the_inputs: Market cap ₹2,680.8 Cr; TTM PAT ₹34.9 Cr; Chapter 5 cases Low ₹20 Cr, Central ₹68 Cr, High ₹131 Cr (FY2029-type full-ramp year).
web_blocks.the_range: 20x: ₹134 Cr; 25x: ₹107 Cr; 30x: ₹89 Cr; 35x: ₹77 Cr; 40x: ₹67 Cr. Only the High case clears 25x; the Central case clears only 40x.
web_blocks.if_off: If the market settles at 20x, the ₹134 Cr hurdle exceeds even the High case, so the equity value would have to fall rather than earnings catch up.

web_blocks.caption: Reverse DCF: earnings needed for a 12% annual return from ₹1,142.20 (our calculation; 12% is an assumption)
web_blocks.takeaway: By March 2029 PAT must reach ₹117-176 Cr, 3.4 to 5.0 times TTM.

web_blocks.html: The grid above sets the hurdle: to earn 12% a year the shares need profit of ₹117 Cr to ₹176 Cr by March 2029, depending on the exit multiple. The next table asks which operating case could deliver it. It pairs each case from Chapter 5 with its profit, its multiple of today's market value, its return on invested capital and the value it supports at 28x.

web_blocks.caption: Which case is priced in? (our calculation; ROIC on about ₹830 Cr of capital, 26% tax, ₹42 Cr depreciation)
headers: Value at 28x on FY2029E EPS (annualised return if reached by March 2029)
web_blocks.takeaway: Management range: dielectric ₹485.5 Cr at 35% EBITDA, Coex ₹370 Cr at 6%, EBITDA about ₹192 Cr.

web_blocks.html: The price corresponds to the High case. At a 28x exit a 12% return needs about ₹126 Cr of FY2029 PAT, 92% of the way from the Central to the High case; at 30x it needs ₹117 Cr. The management-range case returns only about 4% a year at 28x. The High case means Barjora-2 near 90% and the UAE line near 70% utilised, realisation near ₹480/kg and a 40% dielectric margin, against audited ₹383/kg and an implied 16-22% margin in FY2026 (Chapter 5). Management says “One is a volume ramp-up and one is a value ramp-up. They are independent of each other, but both need to happen before we realize the full value” [52]. The price assumes both, on schedule.

web_blocks.title: Peers: who is comparable and what they cost

web_blocks.caption: Xpro India and listed film peers: valuation, profitability and technical snapshot (TradingView scanner, 13 Nov 2026 print)
web_blocks.takeaway: Xpro has the highest P/E in the set (79.3x) while its 3.8% ROCE is above only Polyplex's 0.9%; Jindal Poly is loss-making [10][67].

web_blocks.html: Reading the peers. SRF (32.1x, 18.8% margin) is both a rival, with 4,500 t of capacitor film commissioned in May 2026, and a chemicals group whose multiple is anchored elsewhere [59]. Garware Hi-Tech (41.0x, 20.9% margin) is the closest quality benchmark, with 17-21% margins through the cycle, but in polyester [67]. Cosmo First (10.0x) has a 750 t metallised capacitor line inside a packaging group [60]. Jindal Poly is loss-making after the May 2025 fire, yet its 10,000 t capacity is a direct rival [7]. No listed company is a pure comparable. Per point of ROCE, Xpro pays 20.9 turns of P/E against 2.2 for SRF, 2.3 for Garware and 0.9 for Cosmo, about nine times SRF and Garware; only Polyplex (0.9% ROCE, 19.2x) is as expensive per point, at a quarter of Xpro's P/E (our calculation; a heuristic). We read the premium as a scarcity and option premium on specialty film and a doubling of capacity, not a price for current returns. EV is ₹21.6 lakh per tonne of 13,000 t, against ₹7.6 lakh for Xpro's two new lines and about ₹6.2 lakh for SRF's [59].

web_blocks.title: What multiple is defensible, case by case

web_blocks.html: Our independent view. In the Low case PAT of ₹20 Cr is a 3.0% return on capital, so a P/E is meaningless; we value equity at 1.2x the ₹345 per share of book we estimate for March 2028, or ₹414. In the Central case ROIC is 8.8%, below the 12% cost of capital. In the value-driver identity, P/E = (1 − g ÷ ROIC) ÷ (r − g), such a business is worth at most the no-growth multiple of 1 ÷ 12% = 8.3x, and growth lowers it (6.8x at 4% growth) [107][108]. Our Base 28x is 3.4 times that anchor, already generous, since it pays for upside the Central case does not contain. In the High case ROIC is 16.4%, and 30x needs about 10.9% growth sustained: a long-runway assumption, not a steady state.

Dating convention. Each scenario value in the next table is a price at 31 March 2028 that capitalises FY2029E earnings, a one-year-forward multiple. The reverse-DCF grid above asks a different question. It asks what profit must exist when March 2029 or March 2030 arrives for a 12% annual return. The two use different dates by design, and Chapter 9 uses the March 2028 convention for its probability-weighted value.

web_blocks.caption: Scenario values per share at March 2028 on FY2029E earnings (our calculation; shares 2.347 Cr; PAT before about 15% UAE minority)
web_blocks.takeaway: Only the Bull case is above today's price; the minority share makes all three slightly generous.

web_blocks.html: Base value by multiple: 22x ₹637 (-44.2%), 25x ₹724 (-36.6%), 28x ₹811 (-29.0%), 32x ₹927 (-18.8%); it takes 39.4x, today's market cap over Central PAT, to reach today's price. A 12% annual return to March 2028 would need ₹1,336 (our calculation); only the Bull case clears it.

web_blocks.title: The bull and the skeptic on valuation, each at full strength
paragraphs: Bull: scarcity is real. Xpro is the largest Indian capacitor-film maker, a 13,000 t platform once the UAE line starts, in a market that imports about 70% of its film [53]. Net debt is ₹40 Cr ex-leases against equity of ₹813 Cr, the rating is A-/A1, management does not see a parent equity raise, and Q2 FY27 revenue rose 47% [52]. The UAE line, thin film at ₹600-900/kg and lines 4 and 5 are options; the market cap is only 20.5x the High case's ₹131 Cr.

Skeptic: 76x TTM earnings and 3.5x book on a 3.8% ROCE; even the Central case earns 8.8%, below the 12% hurdle. Indian nameplate is about 22,500 t against 15,000 t of demand [7][59]. Start-up dates slipped 6 to 21 months, the implied dielectric margin is 16-23% against a quoted 35-55%, and euro debt is about 17% hedged. The price pays up front for what the record has not yet shown.

web_blocks.html: What the valuation does and does not support. The price already capitalises the High case and leaves no room for the slippage that has been the pattern; it does not support paying for the Central case. The decision is made in Chapter 9.

We would revisit this valuation if Xpro discloses a dielectric EBITDA margin above 30% with Barjora-2 at 70% or more utilisation, if the UAE line is capitalised by 31 March 2027, or if the shares re-rate down: the ₹811 Base value earns 12% a year only from about ₹694 (our calculation).

book_paragraphs: Let me open with the question under every valuation: what does the price already assume? Ben Graham's old line, which Warren Buffett repeated in his 1987 letter, is that “In the short run, the market is a voting machine but in the long run it is a weighing machine” [106]. This chapter does the weighing for Xpro. A word on dates first. Our verified cutoff is Thursday 12 November 2026, when the shares closed at ₹1,142.20. A later print on Friday, ₹1,190.10, up 4.19% on thin volume, exists, but every number I give you uses the Thursday close unless I say otherwise [40][10].

Start with plain arithmetic. Market capitalisation is price times shares: ₹1,142.20 times 2.347 crore shares, or ₹2,680.8 crore. Add net debt, which is borrowings of ₹273.7 crore plus leases of ₹42.3 crore less cash of ₹233.4 crore, so ₹82.6 crore, and the ₹38.7 crore that belongs to minority holders of the UAE subsidiary, and you get enterprise value, or EV, about ₹2,802 crore. EV is what it would cost to buy the whole business, debts included. Now divide by earnings. Trailing twelve-month earnings per share are ₹15.02, so the price-to-earnings ratio, the P/E, is 76.0 times. On the audited FY2026 EPS of ₹8.19 it is 139.5 times. EV over operating profit of ₹57.5 crore is 48.7 times, EV over sales of ₹591.8 crore is 4.73 times, and price over book value of about ₹330 a share is 3.46 times [5].

Said another way, for every ₹100 you pay you receive about ₹1.30 of annual profit. That would be easier to accept if returns on capital were high. They are not. Return on capital employed is 3.78% and return on equity 2.8% on the Screener data, and the company reports 5.3 to 5.7% for FY2026 [5][104]. Compare that with the 12% cost of capital I assumed in Chapter 6. You are paying three and a half times book value for a business that currently earns well below what its capital costs.

How did we get here? From its listing in April 2004 to March 2020 the share closed between ₹8.5 and ₹55 [40]. Then came fiscal 2022. The close went from ₹48.7 to ₹977.9, twenty-fold, while earnings per share rose about five-fold, from ₹4.72 to ₹25.38. The P/E went from 10.3 times to 38.5 times. Dielectric prices and mix had turned, as Chapter 1 showed, and the market paid a far higher multiple for the new earnings power.

Now watch what happened after earnings peaked. EPS was ₹24.91 in FY2023, then ₹19.91, ₹17.04 and ₹8.19. At each March year-end the P/E was 27.8, 56.1, 68.8 and 123.6 times. The price peaked at ₹1,634.4 on 17 December 2024, fell 50.3% to ₹813.0 on 13 March 2026, bounced to ₹1,503.6 on 2 July, dropped to ₹963.6 on 2 November, and climbed 14.6% after the Q2 results. Set 31 March 2023 beside today: the price is up 65%, while EPS is down 67% on FY2026 and 40% on the trailing twelve months. Every rupee of that gain is a higher multiple. Buffett, quoting Graham again, put it as “Price is what you pay; value is what you get” [109]. The market is paying for the ramp, not for earnings delivered.

So let me turn the question around, the way an investor does with a reverse DCF. Instead of forecasting and then valuing, I ask what has to be true for this price to make sense. If you would pay 25 times for a mature business, ₹2,681 crore of market value needs about ₹107 crore of annual profit. At 40 times it needs ₹67 crore, at 20 times ₹134 crore. Trailing profit is ₹35 crore. In Chapter 5 I built three cases for the full 13,000-tonne platform: Low at ₹20 crore, Central at ₹68 crore and High at ₹131 crore. Only the High case clears the 25-times hurdle.

Now add the return you would want. Assume 12% a year, my hurdle. The price must reach ₹1,499 by March 2029 and ₹1,679 by March 2030. If the market then pays 25 times, earnings per share must be ₹60, which is ₹141 crore of profit in FY2029. At 30 times it is ₹117 crore, at 20 times ₹176 crore. That is 3.4 to 5.0 times what the company earns now, within 2.4 years.

Which case does the price match? Add one more, the management-range case: new-line dielectric revenue of ₹350 crore plus the old line's ₹135.5 crore at a 35% EBITDA margin, and Coex at ₹370 crore and 6%. That gives EBITDA near ₹192 crore and profit near ₹106 crore, so today's market value is 25.3 times it. At a 28-times exit, a 12% return needs about ₹126 crore, 92% of the way from my Central case to my High case. The management-range case would earn about 4% a year. The price therefore corresponds to the High case: both new lines nearly full, thin film near ₹480 a kilogram and a 40% margin, against audited ₹383 and an implied 16 to 22% in FY2026. Management has been candid about the gap: “One is a volume ramp-up and one is a value ramp-up. They are independent of each other, but both need to happen before we realize the full value” [52]. The price assumes both, on schedule.

Here is a point worth slowing down for. Even my Central case earns about ₹73 crore after tax on roughly ₹830 crore of capital, a return of 8.8%, below the 12% cost. A company that earns less than its cost of capital destroys value when it grows. The textbook identity, from Mauboussin and Rappaport's expectations method and Damodaran's work, makes the point exactly: with no growth, a business is worth its earnings divided by its cost of capital, which at 12% is 8.3 times, and growth below the hurdle lowers that [107][108]. My Base multiple of 28 times is therefore 3.4 times the no-growth anchor, and I call it generous because it pays for thin-gauge, UAE and later-line upside that the Central case does not contain. For the High case, with a return of 16.4%, 30 times needs about 10.9% growth sustained for a long time. That is a runway assumption, not a steady state.

Now compare Xpro with its neighbours, with the warning that none is a pure capacitor-film company. SRF trades at 32.1 times earnings with an 18.8% operating margin and a 14.6% return on capital; it is also a rival, with 4,500 tonnes commissioned in May 2026 [59]. Garware Hi-Tech, the best quality benchmark, trades at 41.0 times with a 20.9% margin and an 18.1% return; it held 17 to 21% margins through the cycle but makes polyester film [67]. Cosmo First trades at 10.0 times, Polyplex at 19.3 times, and Jindal Poly Films is loss-making after its 2025 fire. Xpro, on the 13 November print, trades at 79.3 times with a 6.3% operating margin and a 3.8% return on capital.

Divide each P/E by its return on capital and the picture is stark. Xpro pays about 21 turns of P/E for every point of return, SRF about 2.2, Garware 2.3 and Cosmo 0.9. Xpro is about nine times as expensive as SRF and Garware on this crude yardstick. Only Polyplex, with a 0.9% return and a 3.9% margin, is as expensive per point, at a quarter of Xpro's multiple. I read the premium as a scarcity and option premium on specialty capacitor film and on a doubling of capacity, not a price for what the company earns today. One more cross-check: EV of ₹2,802 crore is ₹21.6 lakh per tonne of nameplate, while Xpro's two new lines cost ₹7.6 lakh per tonne and SRF's about ₹6.2 lakh. EV also pays for Coex, but rivals can still add capacity for well under half that value.

So what is each case worth? The Low case, ₹20 crore of profit, is a 3% return, so a P/E means nothing; I value it at 1.2 times the book value I expect by March 2028, about ₹345 a share, which is ₹414, 63.8% below the price. The Base case, ₹68 crore or ₹29 of EPS at 28 times, is ₹811, 29.0% below. The Bull case, ₹131 crore or ₹55.8 of EPS at 30 times, is ₹1,674, 46.6% above. Those profits are before the 15% UAE minority, so all three are slightly generous. Move the Base multiple from 22 to 32 times and the value runs from ₹637 to ₹927, never reaching the price. To earn 12% a year to March 2028 the share would have to be ₹1,336, and only the Bull case clears that.

Let me give the bull his best day. Xpro is the largest Indian capacitor-film maker, with a 13,000-tonne platform once the UAE line starts, in a market that imports about 70% of its film. Net debt is only ₹40 crore against ₹813 crore of equity, the rating is A-, management does not see a parent equity raise, and Q2 revenue rose 47% [52]. The UAE line, thin film at ₹600 to ₹900 a kilogram and the later lines are real options. Management itself says it chose “a slight softening of prices in anticipation of the creation of new capacities” [89], which a bull reads as buying volume ahead of rivals. At the top of the margin range, the High case earns ₹131 crore and today's value is 20.5 times it.

Now the skeptic's best day. Seventy-six times earnings, 3.5 times book, a 3.8% return. Even my Central case earns less than the cost of capital. India has about 22,500 tonnes of nameplate for 15,000 tonnes of demand, every start-up date has slipped by 6 to 21 months, the implied dielectric margin is 16 to 23% against a quoted 35 to 55%, and management accepts price flexibility “even at the risk of occasional impact on margins” [52]. Buffett's 1989 advice was that it is “far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price” [110]. The question is not whether Xpro is a decent business. It is whether this price is fair for it.

My independent view, in a sentence: the price already capitalises the High case and leaves no room for the slippage that has been the pattern, and the Base value of ₹811 is 29% below it. The valuation does not support paying for the Central case. The final decision is made in Chapter 9. What would make me revisit? A disclosed dielectric margin above 30% with the new Indian line at 70% or more utilisation, the UAE line capitalised on schedule by 31 March 2027, or a lower price: the Base value earns 12% a year only from about ₹694.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A price is a forecast somebody else has already made. At ₹1,142 the forecast is that Xpro fills both new lines, sells thinner and dearer film and earns about ₹130 crore, nearly four times what it earns now, and that the market will still pay close to thirty times that profit. You do not need to disagree with the story to see the risk: you only need to notice that the earnings have to arrive on time, and Chapter 5 showed that the calendar is where this management has been weakest.
